title: Characteristic Functions
engineName: Probability — Fourier transforms of probability laws
objectives: Define the characteristic function and explain why it always exists.
Compute CFs for Bernoulli, Poisson, normal and uniform laws.
Use independence, scaling and translation identities.
Recover moments from derivatives when the moments exist.
Apply uniqueness and Lévy continuity to identify distributions and limits.

prereq.name: Independence and sums of random variables
prereq.why: Apply product identities for independent sums.

prereq.name: Taylor expansion and moments
prereq.why: Recover moments by differentiating near zero.

traps: A CF always exists; an MGF may fail to exist near zero.
Independent sums multiply CFs; dependence prevents automatic factorisation.
Equal CFs imply equal distributions; equal moments alone need not.

tricks: Set the CF at zero by continuity when needed.
shortcuts: Poisson rates add by CF multiplication.
A constant c has CF e^{itc}.
remember: CF always exists; MGF need not.
Uniqueness is for CFs, not arbitrary moment sequences.

howto: Start with existence and the three basic properties. Practise Bernoulli, Poisson and uniform examples, then use independence and scaling. Finish with uniqueness and Lévy continuity; these are the main reasons CFs matter beyond computing moments.

provenance: Original syllabus-aligned lesson authored 12 November 2026. Bernoulli, Poisson and uniform CFs and their derivative identities were checked directly from expectations. Independent Poisson sum uses uniqueness of characteristic functions. No PYQ attribution is claimed.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four foundations
scenes.objective: Retrieve expectation, independence and complex exponentials.
body: The characteristic function is the Fourier transform of a probability law.
Unlike an MGF, it exists for every probability distribution because the complex exponential is bounded.

ask.q: What is the modulus of e^{itX} for real t and X?

refresh: The characteristic function is φ_X(t)=E(e^{itX}) and exists for every real t because the integrand has modulus one. For a discrete variable use a probability-weighted sum; for a continuous variable integrate against the density. Keep i²=−1 when simplifying powers.

items.ask: What is independence useful for in a sum?
refresh: Differentiate φ at zero when the relevant moments exist: φ'_X(0)=iE(X) and φ''_X(0)=−E(X²). The alternating powers of i matter. Recover the variance from the first two raw moments rather than treating the second derivative as the variance directly.

items.ask: What is e^{itX} in real and imaginary parts?
refresh: Independence gives φ_(X+Y)(t)=φ_X(t)φ_Y(t). This is the characteristic-function counterpart of MGF factorisation and is useful even when an MGF does not exist. Check independence before multiplying the functions.

Characteristic functions uniquely determine probability distributions. Convergence of characteristic functions to a function continuous at zero supports the continuity theorem; pointwise convergence alone without the continuity condition is not enough to conclude weak convergence.

scenes.title: Why this transform always exists
body: An MGF can fail because E(e^{tX}) diverges. The CF uses e^{itX}, whose modulus is exactly one.
Therefore φ_X(t)=E(e^{itX}) is finite for every real t and every probability law.
For independent sums, CFs multiply. This turns convolution into algebra and supports limit theorems.

scenario.teaser: A heavy-tailed model has no useful MGF, but its characteristic function still exists.
scenario.title: The transform that always exists
body: An MGF can fail because E(e^{tX}) diverges for t>0. The characteristic function uses e^{itX}, whose modulus is exactly one.
Thus φ_X(t)=E(e^{itX}) is finite for every real t, for every probability law. This makes it the universal transform for distributional arguments.
For independent sums, CFs multiply. This turns convolution into algebra and often identifies the sum by matching a known CF.
The normal CF exp(−t²/2) is the target in the classical CLT proof. Lévy's continuity theorem converts pointwise CF convergence into convergence in distribution.
scenario.q: Why does the CF exist even when the MGF fails?
scenario.answer: Because |e^{itX}|=1 for real t, so the integrand is bounded.

ask.q: Why is the CF more universal than the MGF?
ask.nudge: Compare the magnitudes of e^{tX} and e^{itX}.

blocks.body: φ_X(t)=E(e^{itX})=E(cos tX)+iE(sin tX). Since |e^{itX}|=1, the expectation exists for every real t, even when an MGF does not.
φ(0)=1; |φ(t)|≤1; φ(−t)=conjugate φ(t); φ is uniformly continuous and positive definite.
φ_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}φ_X(at). If X,Y are independent, φ_{X+Y}(t)=φ_X(t)φ_Y(t).
Bernoulli(p): 1−p+pe^{it}. Poisson(λ): exp{λ(e^{it}−1)}. Normal(μ,σ²): exp(iμt−σ²t²/2). Uniform(−a,a): sin(at)/(at).
If the rth absolute moment exists, φ^(r)(0)=i^rE(X^r). Thus E(X)=φ'(0)/i and E(X²)=−φ''(0).
A distribution is uniquely determined by its CF. Lévy continuity theorem: pointwise convergence to a function continuous at zero that is a CF gives convergence in distribution to its law.

flow.title: Use a characteristic function
flow.note: The CF always exists; use it when the MGF may fail.

ask.q: What condition allows CFs of a sum to factor?
ask.nudge: The two random variables must satisfy a relationship stronger than zero correlation.

scenes.title: Worked example — add independent Poisson counts
scenes.objective: Use the product rule and uniqueness.
scenes.problem: Let X~Poisson(2), Y~Poisson(3), independent. Find the CF of X+Y and identify its law.
scenes.after: The product rule requires independence. Equal CFs identify the entire distribution.

ask.q: Would the product rule hold automatically if X and Y were dependent?
ask.nudge: The joint expectation would not necessarily factor.

items.a: A characteristic function determines one probability distribution.

scenes.title: Complete the Bernoulli CF
scenes.objective: Recover mean and variance from the CF.
scenes.problem: For Bernoulli(p), complete the characteristic-function calculation.

steps.why: The two support points contribute separately.
At t=0 the derivative is ip.

scenes.after: The CF derivatives recover raw moments when the moments exist.

scenes.title: Moments, uniqueness and continuity
scenes.objective: Use CFs for moments and limit laws.

blocks.body: φ^(r)(0)=i^rE(X^r), when the rth absolute moment exists. Thus E(X)=φ'(0)/i and E(X²)=−φ''(0).
If two probability distributions have the same characteristic function for every real t, they are the same distribution.
If φ_n(t) converges pointwise to φ(t), and φ is continuous at zero, then φ is a characteristic function and the corresponding distributions converge weakly to its law.

ask.q: Why is equality of the first two moments weaker than equality of CFs?
ask.nudge: Many distinct distributions can share a mean and variance.

scenes.title: On your own — Bernoulli moments
scenes.problem: For X~Bernoulli(p=.3), write φ_X(t), then obtain E(X) and Var(X).
scenes.check: Divide φ'(0) by i to obtain the mean; subtract the squared mean for variance.

scenario.teaser: Two independent Poisson sources feed a combined event counter.
scenario.title: Add independent counts without convolution
body: One server generates Poisson(2) events per minute and another independent server generates Poisson(3).
This is the characteristic function of Poisson(5). Uniqueness establishes the distribution, not merely matching moments.
The product rule works for any independent random variables, even if the sum's density or pmf is difficult to calculate directly.
scenario.q: What assumption allows the CFs to multiply?

items.claim: A characteristic function exists for every probability distribution.
Characteristic functions of independent summands multiply.
items.why: True: independence factors the joint expectation.
False: the correct identity is e^{itb}φ_X(at).

items.claim: A characteristic function uniquely determines its distribution.
items.why: True: this is the uniqueness theorem.

scenes.title: Transfer problem — uniform CF
scenes.objective: Integrate the uniform density against the complex exponential.
scenes.problem: For X~Uniform(−π,π), derive φ_X(t) and state its value at t=0.
scenes.check: Define the value at zero by continuity; it is 1, not an undefined ratio.

body: Define the characteristic function and explain why it always exists.
Compute CFs for Bernoulli, Poisson, normal and uniform laws.
Use independence, scaling and translation identities.
Recover moments from derivatives when the moments exist.
